section.title: Jesus Appears and the Ascension
section.sectionRationale: As the disciples talk of the reports, Jesus stands among them and says, Peace be with you. To calm their terror He shows His hands and feet, invites their touch, and eats broiled fish, proving He is risen in body, not a ghost. He opens their minds to understand that all the Scriptures foretold His suffering, rising, and the worldwide preaching of repentance and forgiveness in His name. They are His witnesses, to wait for power from on high. Then He leads them out, blesses them, and is carried up into heaven, and they return to Jerusalem with great joy.
section.thesis: The risen Jesus is truly, bodily alive, the fulfillment of all the Scriptures, who commissions His witnesses to preach repentance and forgiveness to all nations in the power of the Spirit, and who ascends in blessing so that His people worship and wait with great joy.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the bodily appearance to the disciples; the opening of their minds and the commission to be witnesses; and the ascension with blessing, worship, and joy.

units.label: The risen Lord appears in body
units.note: touch Me and see, a spirit has no flesh and bones

verses.text: While they were describing these events, Jesus Himself stood among them and said, “{{eirene|Peace}} be with you.”
But they were startled and frightened, thinking they had seen a spirit.
“Why are you troubled,” Jesus asked, “and why do doubts arise in your hearts?
Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself. Touch Me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have.”
And when He had said this, He showed them His hands and feet.
While they were still in disbelief because of their joy and amazement, He asked them, “Do you have anything here to eat?”
So they gave Him a piece of broiled fish,
and He took it and ate it in front of them.

units.label: The opened mind and the commission
units.note: you are witnesses of these things

verses.text: Jesus said to them, “These are the words I spoke to you while I was still with you: Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.”
Then He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.
And He told them, “This is what is written: The Christ will suffer and rise from the dead on the third day,
and in His name {{metanoia|repentance}} and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem.
And behold, I am sending the promise of My Father upon you. But remain in the city until you have been clothed with {{dynamis|power}} from on high.”

units.label: The ascension
units.note: He blessed them and was carried up into heaven

verses.text: When Jesus had led them out as far as Bethany, He lifted up His hands and blessed them.
While He was blessing them, He left them and was carried up into heaven.
And they worshiped Him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy,
praising God continually in the temple.

eirene.gloss: Peace, the wholeness of the Hebrew shalom. The risen Christ's first word to His frightened disciples is peace, the reconciliation with God that His death and resurrection have secured. To those who had failed and fled, He comes not in reproach but in peace, the fruit of the cross now poured out on His own.

metanoia.gloss: Repentance, a change of mind and turning of the whole life to God. The risen Christ commissions the preaching of repentance and forgiveness in His name to all nations. The gospel calls the world to turn, and offers, in Jesus' name, the pardon that turning receives; this is the mission flowing from the cross and empty tomb.

martys.gloss: Witness, one who testifies to what he has seen. The disciples are witnesses of the suffering, resurrection, and their scriptural fulfillment. Their task is not to invent but to testify, to tell what they have seen and heard of the risen Christ, and the church still stands on their eyewitness testimony.

dynamis.gloss: Power, might. The witnesses are to wait until they are clothed with power from on high, the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. The mission is not carried out by human strength but by the power of God's Spirit, without whom the witnesses could accomplish nothing.

basic.context: As the disciples are still talking about the resurrection reports, Jesus suddenly stands among them and says, Peace be with you. They are terrified, thinking they see a ghost, so He shows them the wounds in His hands and feet, invites them to touch Him, and eats a piece of broiled fish to prove He is truly, bodily alive. Then He tells them that everything written about Him in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms had to be fulfilled, and He opens their minds to understand the Scriptures: the Christ would suffer and rise, and repentance and forgiveness would be preached in His name to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. They are His witnesses, and He will send the promise of the Father, so they must wait in the city until they are clothed with power from on high. Finally He leads them out to Bethany, lifts His hands, blesses them, and is carried up into heaven, and they return to Jerusalem worshiping Him with great joy.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage secures two things: the reality of the bodily resurrection, proved by touch and eating, and the mission that flows from it, grounded in the whole of Scripture. The ascension is not loss but exaltation, and the disciples' joy shows that Christ's departure inaugurates the age of the Spirit and the worldwide gospel.
basic.originalLanguages: The risen Lord's first word is eirene, peace. He commissions the preaching of metanoia, repentance, and forgiveness to all nations. The disciples are His martys, witnesses. And they must wait for dynamis, power, from on high, the coming Spirit.
basic.typology: The risen body of Jesus is the firstfruits of the resurrection all His people await. The blessing with lifted hands echoes the priestly blessing of Aaron, Jesus ascending as the great High Priest. The going up into heaven fulfills the enthronement of the Son of Man at God's right hand.
basic.christ: Jesus is the risen Lord in a real, glorified body, the fulfillment of all the Scriptures, the commissioning King who sends His witnesses, and the ascending High Priest who blesses His people as He is exalted to heaven. His departure is His enthronement.
basic.god: God fulfills every word of the Scriptures in His Son, offers repentance and forgiveness to all nations, and sends the promised Spirit to empower His people. He receives His ascended Son and is worshiped with joy by those who now await the Spirit.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 1 gives the fuller account of the ascension and the promise of the Spirit. Acts 2 records the coming of power at Pentecost. Leviticus 9 shows the priest lifting hands to bless. Psalm 110 seats the ascended Lord at God's right hand.
basic.oneStory: The Gospel closes where the church's mission begins: the risen Christ, truly alive, opens the Scriptures, commissions witnesses to preach repentance and forgiveness to all nations, and ascends in blessing to reign. The story of Jesus flows out into the story of the Spirit-empowered church, and the disciples' great joy is the keynote of the age to come.

context.literary:
These eighteen verses close the Gospel, and Luke has built the ending so that it points forward as much as back. Three scenes follow one another on a single evening and a later day: the appearance in the room, verses 36 to 43, the teaching and commission, verses 44 to 49, and the departure at Bethany, verses 50 to 53. Each one answers a failure in the Gospel's earlier chapters. Terror and doubt are met by flesh and fish. Slowness to understand is met by the opening of the mind. The disciples' flight at the arrest is met by a commission and a promise.

The structure is a descent into the particular and a rise into the universal. The scene opens in a closed room with eleven frightened men and ends with 'all nations,' verse 47, and a Lord lifted into heaven. Luke moves from touch to Scripture to mission to worship, and the final action is the disciples' own: they worship, return and praise.

Luke is careful about contrast. The phrase 'startled and frightened,' verse 37, becomes 'great joy,' verse 52. 'Why do doubts arise in your hearts?' in verse 38 is answered by 'praising God continually' in verse 53. In verse 41 joy and disbelief sit together, 'in disbelief because of their joy and amazement,' which is one of the most human lines in the Gospel.

Verses 44 to 49 are a compressed sermon. They have a clear shape: the Scriptures are fulfilled, the Christ suffers and rises, repentance and forgiveness go out in His name, the disciples are witnesses, and the promise of the Father will clothe them with power. It is the whole of Luke's second volume in outline.

The Gospel ends where it began. Luke 1:8 to 10 opened with a priest in the temple while the people prayed outside. Luke 24:53 ends with the disciples 'praising God continually in the temple.' The same place frames the book, but between the two, the priest who could not speak has been replaced by a people who cannot stop. There is also a priestly gesture at the centre of the last scene: Jesus lifts His hands and blesses, as Aaron once did.
context.historical:
The scene is Sunday evening, the same day as the empty tomb and Emmaus. The disciples are in Jerusalem, afraid, and John adds that the doors were locked 'for fear of the Jews,' John 20:19. Luke does not give the cause, but the whole gathering is under threat. The leaders who had Jesus executed might look for His followers next.

The first thing Jesus says is 'Peace be with you,' the ordinary greeting of the Jewish world, which in Hebrew is shalom. It was an everyday greeting, but on His lips after the cross and the desertion it is also a gift and a forgiveness. The disciples take Him for 'a spirit,' which reflects the widespread belief that the dead might appear as ghosts or disembodied beings. Jesus' answer, 'a spirit does not have flesh and bones,' addresses exactly that belief. The eating of a piece of broiled fish, verse 42, is as deliberately ordinary as possible: no one expects a ghost to be hungry. Peter will later say that the apostles 'ate and drank with Him after He rose from the dead,' Acts 10:41.

The Scriptures He appeals to are the three parts of the Hebrew Bible, 'the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms,' verse 44. The Psalms probably stand here for the third division of the Hebrew canon, since the Psalter is its first and largest book. It is the nearest thing in the New Testament to a naming of the whole Old Testament.

The location of the ascension is Bethany, verse 50, on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles from Jerusalem. Acts 1:12 places the same departure at the Mount of Olives, 'a Sabbath day's journey' away, so the accounts agree on the place. It is the road on which Jesus had entered Jerusalem a week earlier, Luke 19:29 to 37.

The disciples return to a temple in Jerusalem that is still operating. The first Christians continued to worship there, as Acts 2:46 and 3:1 show. They do not yet see themselves as leaving Israel's worship. They are the Jews who believe that its promise has come.
context.canonical:
This closing scene is the pivot between the Gospel and the book of Acts. Luke wrote both, and Acts opens by recalling the first: 'In my first book, O Theophilus, I wrote about all that Jesus began to do and to teach,' Acts 1:1. It then retells the ascension from the other side, with more detail. Acts 1:3 says He appeared 'over a span of forty days,' and Acts 1:9 to 11 describes the cloud and the angels' promise that 'This same Jesus... will come back in the same way you have seen Him go.' Luke 24 compresses the weeks; Acts opens them.

The promise of the Father, verse 49, is the Holy Spirit, and the clothing with power is fulfilled at Pentecost. Acts 2:33 says that, 'exalted to the right hand of God,' Jesus 'has received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what you now see and hear.' John 7:39 had explained that the Spirit could not be given until Jesus was glorified. The ascension is therefore the condition of Pentecost. The prophets looked to such a day: Joel 2:28 and Ezekiel 36:26 to 27.

The mission 'to all nations' recalls the promise to Abraham, 'all nations of the earth will be blessed,' Genesis 22:18, and Isaiah's servant who is a light 'for the nations,' Isaiah 49:6. Luke had heard Simeon say that in Luke 2:32, and Acts 1:8 tells of a witness 'to the ends of the earth.' 'Beginning in Jerusalem' shows that the gospel begins with the place that had rejected Him, a mark of grace.

The lifting of hands to bless belongs to the priestly world. 'Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them,' Leviticus 9:22, and the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24 to 26 closes with 'peace.' The ascending Christ is also the great high priest who 'has passed through the heavens,' Hebrews 4:14, and who 'entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf,' Hebrews 9:24. Psalm 110:1, which Jesus quoted in Luke 20:42, and Daniel 7:13 supply the enthronement. Paul draws on Psalm 68 for the ascent and the gifts, Ephesians 4:8 to 10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wanted to leave no doubt that the risen Christ is a real, embodied person, and that what the church proclaims did not start as a vision or a feeling. He gives three kinds of evidence in the short space of verses 39 to 43: sight, touch and food. The point is not that physical proof produces faith, since verse 41 shows that even with the proof they were still struggling. It is that the message they will take to the world concerns a risen man, not an idea.

His second purpose is to tie the resurrection to Scripture and to mission. Verse 44's 'everything must be fulfilled' and verse 46's 'this is what is written' insist that nothing in the story is improvised. Then the sentence runs on without a pause: 'in His name repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations.' The resurrection is not a private comfort; it is a public commission. Luke wants his readers to see that the church's preaching comes from the risen Lord's own mouth.

His third purpose is to show that the departure of Jesus is not an ending but a handover. The Gospel ends with a blessing, not a farewell, and with a people who are joyful and in the temple, not mourning. Luke wants his readers, many of them Gentiles far from Jerusalem, to see themselves as the 'all nations' of verse 47 and to read their own faith as the continuation of what he narrates.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much in this passage is unique and is not a pattern for believers. Jesus' showing of His wounds, the eating of fish and the visible ascension were events given to the apostles as witnesses. Nobody is told to look for repeats of them. The commands in the passage are limited too: 'remain in the city' was an instruction for the Eleven in the days before Pentecost, and Acts 2 records that it was kept. Later believers are not commanded to wait in Jerusalem but are given the Spirit as promised.

What does carry over is the commission and the pattern. The proclamation of repentance and forgiveness in Christ's name to all nations is not a description of one sermon but the standing task of His people. The witness is the apostles' in a special sense, verse 48, because they saw, but the work of testifying continues, as Acts shows. The disciples' response, worship and continual praise, is also a pattern more than a command.

Caution is needed with 'touch Me and see.' It is not a prescription for believers to demand physical proof, and Jesus tells Thomas, in John 20:29, 'Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.' The scene describes how the Lord gave the first witnesses what they needed, and the rest of us believe through their witness.

debates.question: How do the accounts of the ascension in Luke 24 and Acts 1 fit together?

views.label: They describe the same event, with Luke 24 compressing the timeline
views.case: Luke 24 reads as though the appearance in the room, the teaching and the departure happened on one evening. Acts 1:3 says appearances lasted forty days. On this view Luke deliberately compresses in the Gospel's last chapter and expands in Acts, using the Gospel's close as a summary and not a diary. Both end at Bethany or the Mount of Olives and both have a blessing and a departure.

views.label: There are two phases of the same ascending, one on resurrection day and one at forty days
views.case: A smaller number suggest that Jesus ascended to the Father on Easter day, as John 20:17 may hint, and returned for further appearances before a final visible departure at forty days. The text does not state this, so it is an attempt to harmonise a real tension.

views.label: Luke is writing two versions for different purposes
views.case: Others say Luke did not mean the Gospel's chapter to be read as a timetable and that the two accounts have different emphases, one on the commission and one on the promise, and need not be forced into a single sequence.

debates.bearing: The simplest reading is that Luke ended the Gospel with a summary and filled in the period in Acts, since in both accounts the same elements recur: the Scriptures, the promise of the Spirit, the witness and the departure. The point of both is the same, that the risen Lord is exalted and sends His church.

debates.question: What kind of body does the risen Jesus have?

views.label: The same physical body, raised and restored
views.case: Jesus invites touch, shows wounds, and eats. He says 'flesh and bones.' This is the body that was buried, now alive, and it has not been replaced by a different kind of thing. Many in the early church stressed this against those who said that the resurrection was only spiritual.

views.label: A transformed, glorified body, with continuity but new powers
views.case: Jesus appears suddenly when doors are locked, John 20:19, and vanishes from the table in verse 31. Paul speaks of a 'spiritual body,' 1 Corinthians 15:44, not meaning immaterial but fitted for the Spirit's life. On this view the same body is made new.

views.label: A visionary or purely spiritual presence
views.case: Some modern readers think the appearances were inward experiences. They say that verses 39 to 43 are Luke's way of guarding against the claim of a ghost.

debates.bearing: Luke's own emphasis excludes the third, since he insists on flesh, bones and eating. The first two are not far apart: both affirm continuity with the crucified body. The text says what it says, that He is no ghost, and leaves the physics of the glorified body open.

study.originalLanguages:
The Greek of these verses supplies several details that the English can only hint at, beyond the words the study already marks.

In verse 37 they thought they had seen a 'spirit,' a word for a disembodied being, and in verse 39 Jesus tells them to 'touch' Him. The verb for touch is a strong one meaning to feel over, to handle, to grope. It is the word John uses in 1 John 1:1 when he says that 'our hands have touched' the Word of life, and in Acts 17:27 Paul uses it of people who 'grope' for God. Jesus does not offer a glance; He invites a thorough examination.

His phrase 'flesh and bones' is deliberately concrete. Nothing is said about blood, and Luke does not say how this body is sustained. What matters is solidity.

Verse 41 says they 'were still in disbelief because of their joy.' The verb 'to disbelieve' is the same one used of the apostles' reaction to the women in verse 11, and now the cause has changed: it is not nonsense but the shock of something too good to be true. This is a psychological detail Luke notes with care.

In verse 44 'everything must be fulfilled' uses the verb for necessity again, the same idea as in verse 26. 'Fulfilled' means filled up or brought to completion, so what Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms wrote is not merely foretold but brought to its full measure.

Verse 45 says He 'opened their minds,' using the same verb as verses 31 and 32, which means to open fully. The noun for mind is the faculty of understanding. In Acts 16:14 the same verb is used of Lydia's heart. So the Lord opens eyes, Scriptures and minds in the same chapter. 'To understand' is a compound verb that means to put together, to grasp the sense of the Scriptures as a whole.

Verse 47 says repentance and forgiveness 'will be proclaimed.' The verb is the one for a herald's announcement. 'Forgiveness' is a noun meaning release, which Luke used in Luke 4:18 of the 'liberty to the captives' Jesus came to proclaim. The Gospel which began with release proclaimed in Nazareth ends with release proclaimed to all nations. Then the participle 'beginning' is grammatically loose: it is in the plural and most naturally attaches to the 'you' of verse 48, so that it reads 'beginning from Jerusalem, you are witnesses.' That small point puts the apostles at the head of the mission.

In verse 49 'I am sending' is a present tense with a future sense, and the 'promise of My Father' is a standard expression for the Holy Spirit in Luke and Acts, Acts 1:4. 'Remain' translates a verb that literally means to sit, and the image of 'being clothed with power' is the language of the Old Testament, where the Spirit 'clothes' a person, as in Judges 6:34, where the Hebrew verb means 'clothed,' though the BSB renders it 'came upon.'

In verse 51 He 'was carried up,' an imperfect passive, 'was being carried up' as He was blessing them. The blessing is not interrupted; it is ongoing as He departs. A small number of ancient manuscripts omit the words 'and was carried up into heaven,' and also 'worshiped Him' in verse 52, but the overwhelming majority have both, and Acts 1:9 confirms the event.

Finally, the verb for 'bless' occurs three times in verses 50 to 53: He blesses them, and they, at the end, are 'blessing' God. The same word travels from His mouth to theirs.

typology.fulfillment: 'Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them,' after the sacrifices were made, Leviticus 9:22. At the close of Luke, Jesus lifts His hands and blesses the disciples after the one sacrifice has been made. The correspondence is the raised hands and the blessing after atonement. The escalation is that Aaron then stepped down and went about his work, while Jesus is carried up and does not step down. Hebrews 9:24 says He 'entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God.' The type falls short because Aaron blessed Israel for a day, while Christ's blessing is for all nations and for good.

Elijah was taken up into heaven in a whirlwind while Elisha watched, and a double portion of his spirit rested on Elisha, 2 Kings 2:9 to 15. The disciples likewise watch their Master go up and are told to wait for power. The resemblance is the departure and the promise of the Spirit for the successor. The difference is that Elijah was carried off and did not return or intercede, and he did not rise from death. Jesus ascends as the one who died and rose, and He does not leave a successor but sends the Spirit, who is the Spirit of Christ Himself.

typology.type: The Son of Man enthroned, Daniel 7:13 to 14
typology.fulfillment: Daniel saw 'One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven' brought before the Ancient of Days and given dominion over all peoples. Luke's ascension carries a man up into heaven, and Acts 1:9 adds that 'a cloud hid Him from their sight.' The vision of Daniel is the final meaning of the event: the Son of Man receives the kingdom. Acts 2:33 says He is 'exalted to the right hand of God.' The type is exceeded in that Daniel saw it in vision, and Luke saw it with eyes, and that this king bears wounds.

The Old Testament presented the firstfruits, the first sheaf, as a pledge of the harvest to come, Leviticus 23:10 to 11. The risen body shown in the room, which can be touched and fed, is the first of its kind. Paul says 'Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.' The correspondence is that the first part guarantees the rest, which makes the disciples' fleshly encounter an assurance about their own future. It falls short only in that the harvest is not yet in, and creation still groans, Romans 8:23.

study.christ:
The passage presents Christ as the one in whom everything written comes to completion. 'Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms,' He says, and then He opens their minds to see it. He does not simply have a place in the Old Testament; He is the fullness of what it was reaching for. The sufferings, the rising on the third day and the preaching to the nations are all written, verse 46 and 47. This is the claim that the whole Bible has one center, as John 5:39 also says of the Scriptures, 'These are the very words that testify about Me.'

He is the risen Lord in a true body. The wounds, the touch and the fish show that the resurrection is not an escape from the body but the redemption of it, and so the hope of believers is bodily too. Paul draws the connection when he says Christ is 'the firstfruits,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, and Philippians 3:21 says He 'will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.' Because He is risen in the flesh, the world is not abandoned and matter is not the enemy.

He is the commissioning King. 'You are witnesses,' He tells them. He speaks not as a departing teacher but as the one with authority over the nations: repentance and forgiveness will be preached 'in His name.' The forgiveness of sins, which belongs to God alone, now flows through the name of Jesus. Peter says plainly, 'Salvation is found in no one else,' Acts 4:12.

He is the giver of the Spirit. 'I am sending the promise of My Father upon you.' The one who was conceived by the Spirit, anointed by the Spirit and led by the Spirit now sends the Spirit. John the Baptist had said that He would baptize with the Holy Spirit, Luke 3:16. It is a divine prerogative that He exercises.

He is the priest who blesses and the king who is enthroned. With raised hands He blesses, and as He blesses He is taken up. The same Jesus who offered Himself now intercedes: Hebrews 7:25 says 'He always lives to intercede.' The ascension is therefore not a retreat but an enthronement, as Acts 2:33 and Philippians 2:9 say. The risen Lord is on the throne, and the history of the world is in the hands of the One who was crucified.

We should not turn the passage into an allegory. Luke does not say that the fish are a symbol or that the eleven are types of something. The ordinary points are enough: He is truly risen, He is the fulfillment of the Scriptures, He commissions, He sends the Spirit and He reigns.
study.god:
The God of this passage is the God who keeps His word across the whole Bible. The phrase 'everything must be fulfilled' covers centuries of promise, and the way Jesus opens the Scriptures shows that nothing in the story took God by surprise. The cross and resurrection were not a rescue after a failure but the plan He had been unfolding. Acts 2:23 says that Jesus was delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge. The God of Israel and the Father of Jesus are one God, whose promises are kept.

He is a God who gives peace before He gives instruction. The first thing the risen Lord says to a room of men who had deserted Him is 'Peace be with you.' He does not open with a reproach. The reconciliation is the ground on which the commission stands, which is the order of the gospel everywhere, as Paul says in Romans 5:1 that we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.

He is a God of the body. He made flesh, and in the resurrection He does not discard it. The risen Jesus eats, and the New Testament future is not escape from creation but its renewal, Romans 8:21. This is a God who loves matter and who redeems what He made.

He is a God who opens minds. The gift of understanding comes from Him, as the opening of eyes, Scriptures and minds in this chapter show. We cannot reason ourselves into recognizing the Lord. Paul says that the natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit, 1 Corinthians 2:14, and Luke shows the Lord overcoming that.

He is a God of all nations. The commission to preach to 'all nations' fulfills the promise to Abraham that in his seed all the nations would be blessed, Genesis 12:3. The God of Israel was always the God of the whole earth, and the scope of the gospel makes this public.

He is the God who sends the Spirit and who is present with His people. The promise of the Father is not an addition but the presence of God Himself with His church. The one who dwelt in the tabernacle and the temple now clothes His people with power. And He is the God who receives worship: the disciples 'worshiped Him,' verse 52. In Luke 4:8 Jesus had said, 'Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only,' so when the disciples worship Jesus without rebuke here, Luke has put Him on the side of God.

For worship, the response of the passage is the right one: great joy and continual praise. A people who have been given peace, sight, understanding, a mission and the Spirit have every reason to be found in the temple praising God. And because Jesus has been taken up, our praise is addressed to One who is present, though unseen.

crossReferences.note: Luke's own second volume retells the ascension with more detail: forty days of appearances, the promise of the Spirit, the cloud and the angels' word that He will return in the same way. It shows that Luke 24 is a compressed ending and that the two books overlap deliberately at the point of handover.

Peter says that Jesus, exalted to the right hand of God, has received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and poured it out. It shows how the ascension in verse 51 and the promise in verse 49 are linked: the exaltation is what makes the gift of the Spirit possible.

John's account of the same evening has Jesus enter the locked room, say 'Peace be with you,' and show His hands and side. The agreement of two independent traditions on the greeting, the wounds and the doubting reaction confirms that Luke is not inventing the scene, and Thomas's confession, 'My Lord and my God,' answers it.

John writes that what we have heard, seen and touched with our hands concerns the Word of life. It is the apostolic testimony of verse 48 stated from the inside: the church preaches what was handled and seen, which is why the passage insists on flesh and bones.

After the sacrifices, Aaron lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them. Luke's ending has the same picture: the raised hands, the blessing, and the one who offered the sacrifice. It invites the reader to see Jesus as the priest of whom Aaron was a shadow.

God promised Abraham that through his offspring all nations of the earth would be blessed. The commission of verse 47 to preach to all nations is the unfolding of this promise, and Paul reads the offspring as Christ, Galatians 3:16. The ascending Christ blessing His people stands at the center of that promise.

'Sit at My right hand' is the psalm Jesus Himself applied to the Christ in Luke 20:42 to 43. The ascension is the moment at which the seat is taken, and Peter quotes it in Acts 2:34 to 35. It is the main Old Testament passage that interprets the going up of verse 51 as enthronement.

Christ did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary but heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God. It explains what the Lord is doing when He leaves: He goes as priest into the real sanctuary, so that the blessing of verse 50 continues.

The Gospel opens with Zechariah serving as priest in the temple while the whole congregation prays outside. Luke 24:53 closes with the disciples in the temple praising God. The matching frame shows how the story that began in a priest's silence ends in a people's praise.

Paul quotes a psalm of the conquering king who ascends and gives gifts, and applies it to Christ, who 'ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things.' It gives a theology of the ascension that Luke only describes: the departure is a filling, and the gifts to His people include the Spirit.

study.oneStory:
This passage closes a story that began with the first rupture in Genesis. When Adam and Eve hid, God came looking for them in the garden, and He has been coming ever since, through Abraham, Moses, the prophets and finally His Son. Here the risen Son comes into a locked room and says 'Peace be with you.' The first thing the story had lost, peace between God and His people, is the first thing He gives back.

It shows how the Bible's separate threads are tied together. Everything 'written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms' converges on one person, and the opening of the disciples' minds is what makes it possible to read the whole as one story. The promise of a seed in Genesis 3:15, the blessing of the nations in Genesis 12:3 and the suffering servant of Isaiah are not separate hopes but one hope, now seen in its fulfillment.

It also looks ahead. The promise of the Father points to Pentecost, and from there to the church's mission, which fills the rest of Acts and the rest of history. Jesus will be preached 'to all nations,' and wherever the message goes, it brings repentance and forgiveness. The church is the sign that the blessing promised to Abraham is on its way to every people. The disciples return to Jerusalem, wait, and then go out.

And it points to the end. The angels' promise in Acts 1:11 is that this same Jesus will come back. The hands that were lifted in blessing will be seen again. The bodily resurrection of Jesus is the pledge that the creation itself will be renewed, so that 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3, and the One who ascended is the One who will return and make all things new. Until then the story is carried by joyful witnesses who worship and wait, and whose whole life is lived under the blessing of the ascended Lord.

quiz.q: How does Jesus prove to the frightened disciples that He is truly risen?

options.text: He shows them His hands and feet, invites their touch, and eats broiled fish before them.
options.note: Luke 24:39-43 gives the bodily proofs of touch and eating.

options.text: He shows them the wounds in His hands and feet.
options.note: True, but it omits the further proof of eating food to show He is not a ghost.

options.text: He explains that He is a spirit returned from the dead.
options.note: The opposite: He insists a spirit has no flesh and bones, as He does.

options.text: He simply tells them to believe without any proof.
options.note: He offers concrete physical evidence of His bodily resurrection.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say the Scriptures foretold about Him?

options.text: That the Christ would suffer and rise, and that repentance and forgiveness would be preached to all nations in His name.
options.note: Luke 24:46-47 unites His suffering and rising with the worldwide mission.

options.text: That the Christ would suffer and rise from the dead on the third day.
options.note: True, but it omits the worldwide preaching of repentance and forgiveness that follows.

options.text: That the Messiah would reign over Israel in glory.
options.note: The stress here is on suffering, rising, and the mission to all nations, not national glory.

options.text: That the Scriptures had little to say about Him.
options.note: He says everything written about Him in all the Scriptures must be fulfilled.

quiz.q: What are the disciples commissioned and told to do?

options.text: To be witnesses and to wait in the city until they are clothed with power from on high.
options.note: Luke 24:48-49 gives both the witness role and the command to await the Spirit.

options.text: To be witnesses of Jesus' death and resurrection.
options.note: True, but it omits the command to wait for the promised power of the Spirit.

options.text: To go out immediately in their own strength.
options.note: They are told to wait for power from on high before going.

options.text: To keep the news within Jerusalem alone.
options.note: The mission is to all nations, beginning at Jerusalem, not confined to it.

options.text: Jesus lifts His hands, blesses them, and is carried up into heaven while blessing them.
options.note: Luke 24:50-51 shows the priestly blessing and the ascension.

options.text: Jesus is taken up into heaven before the disciples.
options.note: True, but it omits that He ascended in the very act of blessing them with lifted hands.

options.text: Jesus quietly disappears without a word.
options.note: He ascends openly while blessing them, not by silent vanishing.

options.text: Jesus departs, leaving the disciples in despair.
options.note: They return with great joy, not despair.

quiz.q: How do the disciples respond after Jesus ascends?

options.text: They worship Him and return to Jerusalem with great joy, praising God continually in the temple.
options.note: Luke 24:52-53 records worship, joy, and continual praise.

options.text: They return to Jerusalem filled with joy.
options.note: True, but it omits their worship of Jesus and continual praise in the temple.

options.text: They scatter to their homes in confusion.
options.note: The opposite: they gather in joyful worship, awaiting the Spirit.

options.text: They mourn the loss of their teacher.
options.note: They rejoice, for the ascension is His exaltation, not a loss.

questions: The risen Jesus greeted His failed disciples with, Peace be with you. How does it change you to know that Christ meets those who have failed Him not with reproach but with peace?
Jesus proved His resurrection was bodily, touchable, real. How does the physical reality of His rising strengthen your hope for your own resurrection and the renewal of all things?
He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. Where do you need Christ to open your understanding of His word, rather than trying to grasp it by effort alone?
The disciples were told to wait for power from on high before going. Are you trying to serve God in your own strength, when He offers the power of His Spirit?

Jesus ascended while blessing His people, and they returned with great joy. Does the reign of the ascended Christ fill your daily life with that kind of worship and joy, and if not, what has crowded it out?

translationNotes.note: In 'Touch Me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones', Jesus insists on the bodily reality of His resurrection against the thought that He is a ghost.
'The Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms' names the three divisions of the Hebrew Scriptures, a way of saying the whole Old Testament bears witness to Christ.

The 'promise of My Father' and 'power from on high' are the Holy Spirit, sent at Pentecost as recorded in Acts 2. Luke ends his Gospel with the ascension and picks up the same events at the start of Acts, binding the two volumes together.
